summary: The model predicts the chance of a low income (the lower of the dataset's income classes); over the 39073 training rows its mean predicted chance is 75.5% against an outcome rate of 76.1%. It is mostly a linear score: switching the direct linear terms off lowers the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.748. Through their own edges, capital gains, education level, being married to a civilian spouse, being a husband or a wife, being a man and working more hours lower the predicted chance, and living as a child of the household raises it. Two nonlinear parts come next by ablation: people aged 34 years or younger (16819 rows) get a push towards a low income that grows the younger they are, and capital gains above a threshold between 5200 US dollars and 5300 US dollars (typical person; 1757 rows with the hinge open) lower it well beyond the direct capital-gains term. Small single-category gates raise it for private-household service workers (187 rows) and China-born people (96 rows), raise it for handlers or cleaners, and lower it for technical-support workers and doctorate holders; a chain on race is inactive on the training data. The annotated model reproduces the original to within 5.0e-16.
